learningObjective: Distinguish 'symbolic shape' (a compile-time symbolic representation of an unknown extent) from 'dynamic shape' (a runtime-unknown extent) and identify their design implications.

canonicalClaims.claim: 'Dynamic shape' is the property that a dim's extent is not known statically; 'symbolic shape' is a representation technique that uses named symbols (with optional constraints such as positivity, divisibility, or inter-dim relations) at compile time to reason about that unknown dim.
conditions: The compiler has some notion of compile-time symbols for dims.
nonImplications: Does not imply symbolic-shape support automatically covers all possible dynamic inputs; symbols may carry constraints.
Does not imply symbolic shapes are free at compile time; symbol propagation and constraint solving have their own cost.

misconceptions.claim: Symbolic shape and dynamic shape are synonyms.
misconceptions.whyWrong: One is a property (dynamic), the other a representation technique (symbolic).

misconceptions.claim: Symbolic shape means the tensor's underlying memory is symbolic.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Memory allocation is a separate concern; symbolic shape is about compile-time reasoning over dim symbols.

misconceptions.claim: A compiler always uses either symbolic or dynamic shape, never both together.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Symbolic shape is the standard way to model dynamic shape in compilers such as Relax and PyTorch's Dynamo.

misconceptions.claim: Symbolic shape refers to dtype variation across runs.

implementationFacts: TVM Relax: symbolic dim variables with constraints
PyTorch: SymInt / SymFloat used by Dynamo and AOTAutograd
MLIR: shape dialect / dynamic dims via `?` in tensor/memref types
performanceScenarios: Symbolic-shape compilation enables one compiled artifact to serve many input shapes, reducing recompilation cost at the price of some codegen specialization.
